title: Microbiology Paper 3: Pathogens, Sterilisation and Immunity
source: Adapted from user-provided Dentistry past paper questions (Microbiology pages)

objective.question: Which of the following microorganisms is an RNA virus?
objective.explanation: Rabies virus is a member of the Rhabdoviridae family and carries a single-stranded RNA genome; pox, herpes and papova viruses are DNA viruses.

objective.question: Which of the following microorganisms is known for spore formation?
objective.explanation: Clostridium species are classic endospore-forming Gram-positive bacilli; the other genera listed do not form spores.

objective.question: Which of the following organisms is responsible for pyogenic infections?
objective.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is a leading pus-forming (pyogenic) pathogen of skin and soft tissue; the oral species listed are not typically pyogenic.

objective.question: Which of the following is not used during Gram staining?
objective.explanation: Gram staining uses crystal violet, Gram's iodine, an alcohol or acetone decolouriser and a counterstain; chloroform is not part of the procedure.

objective.question: A facultative parasite lives:
options: Both outside and inside the host
objective.explanation: A facultative parasite can live freely in the environment but can also infect and live on or in a host, unlike an obligate parasite.

objective.question: Which mosquito species is the principal vector of Plasmodium falciparum transmission in Africa?
objective.explanation: Female Anopheles mosquitoes, such as Anopheles gambiae, transmit human Plasmodium species; Aedes and Culex species transmit other arboviruses.

objective.question: Which of the following is the most reliable method of sterilising heat-sensitive items such as disposable plastic syringes?
objective.explanation: Membrane filtration removes microorganisms from heat-sensitive liquids without heat, making it the reliable choice for heat-labile materials.

objective.question: The basic reproductive number (R0) of an infection describes:
options: The percentage of the population that must be vaccinated
The average number of new cases generated by one infected person in a fully susceptible population
The time from infection to the onset of symptoms
The proportion of infected people who die from the disease
objective.explanation: R0 is the average number of secondary infections produced by a single infected individual in a wholly susceptible population; herd immunity thresholds are derived from it.

objective.question: Which of the following is the main route of transmission of rotavirus infection in children?
options: Faecal-oral spread through contaminated hands and surfaces
objective.explanation: Rotavirus spreads mainly by the faecal-oral route via contaminated hands, surfaces and food, causing acute gastroenteritis in young children.

objective.question: Which of the following fungi species is responsible for hair loss?
objective.explanation: Trichophyton species are dermatophytes that invade hair, skin and nails and are a common cause of tinea involving hair loss.

objective.question: The fungus that commonly causes athlete's foot (tinea pedis) belongs to the group of:
objective.explanation: Dermatophytes (e.g. Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum) digest keratin and cause superficial infections of skin, hair and nails.

objective.question: Pasteurisation is primarily used to:
options: Destroy all spores in a liquid
Kill pathogens while preserving the quality of food and beverages
Sterilise surgical instruments for theatre use
objective.explanation: Pasteurisation heats liquids to a temperature below 100°C for a set time to destroy pathogens and spoilage organisms while preserving flavour and nutrients.

objective.question: Which antibody is normally present in high concentration in secretions such as saliva, tears and breast milk?
objective.explanation: Secretory IgA is the dominant antibody of mucosal secretions and provides local immunity at entry sites of the body.

objective.question: Tolerance to the body's own antigens is ensured partly by:
options: Clonal deletion of self-reactive lymphocytes during their development
Production of IgE by mast cells
Activation of complement by the alternative pathway
Phagocytosis of red blood cells by the liver
objective.explanation: Self-reactive lymphocyte clones are eliminated (clonal deletion) during maturation, so the immune system does not attack the body's own tissues.

objective.question: Active immunity differs from passive immunity in that active immunity:
options: Gives immediate protection after an antibody injection
Results from the individual's own immune response and produces immunological memory
objective.explanation: Active immunity develops after infection or vaccination, involves the person's own lymphocytes and leaves immunological memory; passive immunity is short-lived borrowed antibody.

objective.question: Which of the following is a non-specific (innate) defence reaction of the body?
options: Production of specific antibodies against tetanus toxoid
Inflammation characterised by redness, heat, swelling and pain
Formation of memory B cells after vaccination
Rejection of a graft by sensitised T lymphocytes
objective.explanation: Inflammation is a rapid, non-specific innate response; the other options are specific (adaptive) immune responses.

objective.question: The tuberculin (Mantoux) skin test detects:
options: Circulating IgE antibodies in the blood
Delayed-type hypersensitivity to tuberculin in a previously sensitised person
Active multiplication of tubercle bacilli at the time of the test
Immunity conferred by BCG vaccination alone
objective.explanation: The Mantoux test reads a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction to purified protein derivative, indicating prior sensitisation to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

objective.question: A plasmid is best defined as:
options: The main chromosome of a bacterial cell
A small extra-chromosomal DNA molecule that can replicate independently
A segment of DNA that codes for ribosomal RNA
A viral genome permanently fused to the cell wall
objective.explanation: Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules separate from the bacterial chromosome that replicate autonomously and often carry antibiotic-resistance genes.

objective.question: A mosquito that carries Plasmodium from one human to another is best classified as a:
objective.explanation: A biological vector not only transports the parasite but also supports part of its development, which is why Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria.

objective.question: The term 'pyogenic' means:
objective.explanation: Pyogenic organisms are pus formers; Staphylococcus aureus and pyogenic streptococci are typical examples.

structured.question: List four (4) routes by which nosocomial (healthcare-associated) infections may be transmitted and give one example of each. (4 marks)
markingGuide: Direct contact transmission, e.g. hand transfer of Staphylococcus aureus to a wound
Indirect contact via contaminated instruments or equipment, e.g. reused dental handpieces
Droplet or airborne transmission, e.g. Mycobacterium tuberculosis in aerosols
Vector-borne or faecal-oral transmission, e.g. contaminated food or water in the hospital
structured.modelAnswer: Nosocomial infections spread by direct contact (infected hands or wounds), indirect contact through contaminated instruments and surfaces, droplet/airborne spread from coughing or aerosol-generating procedures, and faecal-oral or vector-borne transfer of enteric organisms such as Salmonella.

structured.question: Mention four (4) articles contaminated by Salmonella Typhi. (4 marks)
markingGuide: Contaminated drinking water
Food such as milk, salads or street-vended foods
Bed linen and towels of a carrier or patient
Cutlery, plates and eating utensils
structured.modelAnswer: Salmonella Typhi is shed in urine and faeces of patients and carriers and contaminates water, food, bed linen and eating utensils, which then serve as vehicles of transmission.

structured.question: Identify four (4) major species of Plasmodium in man. (4 marks)
markingGuide: Plasmodium falciparum
Plasmodium vivax
Plasmodium malariae
Plasmodium ovale
structured.modelAnswer: The four major human malaria parasites are Plasmodium falciparum (the most dangerous), Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium malariae and Plasmodium ovale; Plasmodium knowlesi is a less common zoonotic species.

structured.question: State four (4) factors that should be considered when selecting an antimicrobial drug for a patient. (4 marks)
markingGuide: Identity and susceptibility of the causative organism
Severity and site of the infection
Patient factors such as age, pregnancy, allergies and kidney or liver function
Spectrum of action, dosage form, cost and availability of the drug
structured.modelAnswer: Choice of an antimicrobial depends on laboratory identification and sensitivity of the organism, the site and severity of infection, patient-related factors (age, allergy, pregnancy, renal/hepatic function, immune status), and drug factors including spectrum, pharmacokinetics, cost and availability.

structured.question: List four (4) disease causal agents, naming the organism and the disease it causes. (4 marks)
markingGuide: Mycobacterium tuberculosis - tuberculosis
Plasmodium falciparum - malaria
Salmonella Typhi - enteric (typhoid) fever
Candida albicans - oral candidiasis
structured.modelAnswer: Examples include Mycobacterium tuberculosis causing tuberculosis, Plasmodium falciparum causing malaria, Salmonella Typhi causing enteric fever and Candida albicans causing oral candidiasis.
